name: Black-market / DIY fillers

card.summary: Filler bought outside regulated channels and injected without a clinician; the practice exists on forums, and the main risks are those regulators and reviewers attach to all fillers, with no safeguards.
card.note: Vascular occlusion, including blindness and tissue death, is a documented complication of filler injection even in clinical settings.

quick.overview:
Black-market or DIY filler refers to dermal filler products that people obtain outside licensed medical channels and inject into their own faces. On looksmaxxing forums it is presented as a way to enhance the jaw, chin or lips without visiting a clinic.

The forum material consists of user guides and personal plans, not research. Published sources on dermal fillers describe the injection of fillers by trained providers; no studies of self-injection were identified.
quick.mechanism: Users describe injecting hyaluronic acid-type gels of different firmness to add structure or soften transitions in areas such as the jaw, chin and lips. Fillers in general work by adding volume at the injection site.
quick.risks: Reference sources describe bruising, redness and pain as common effects of dermal fillers, and rare but serious complications including blindness caused by material reaching the eye's arteries, usually permanent when it occurs [1]. In the US, fillers are regulated as devices that a provider must inject [1]. Forum posters themselves discuss vascular occlusion and nerve injury as risks.

lead: Black-market or DIY filler is the practice of buying injectable dermal filler outside regulated medical supply and administering it to oneself, as described on looksmaxxing forums. It overlaps with the broader topic of unlicensed injection of fat-dissolving agents and botulinum toxin, which some users discuss in the same threads [4].

Reference sources state that in the United States dermal fillers are approved as medical devices and a provider must prescribe and perform the injection, while in the UK and EU they are non-prescription devices under a CE mark that does not itself require proof of efficacy [1]. Wikipedia's overview lists bruising, redness and pain as common effects of fillers, infection and allergic reactions as less common, and blindness from retrograde embolization into the ophthalmic and retinal arteries as rare but typically permanent [1].
No published study of self-injected filler was identified. Material about the practice comes almost entirely from forum posts, which this article describes only in general terms.

paras: On looksmax.org, threads on DIY filler include a long guide posted under a disclaimer that it neither promotes nor condones the practice, which lists the supplies, safety rules and warning signs its author considers essential [2]. The guide distinguishes firmer fillers intended to add structure from softer ones intended to smooth transitions, and mentions microcannulas and hyaluronidase as tools to reduce risk or reverse hyaluronic acid filler [2]. This article does not reproduce procedural details.

Other posters describe personal plans, for example a user who said he had ordered filler for the chin, a fat-dissolving product and botulinum toxin online and intended to study anatomy before self-injecting [4]. A teenage poster asked whether jaw-widening filler would look unnatural as his face continued to grow [3].

Wikipedia's dermal filler overview states that vision loss can follow injection when material travels back into the arteries supplying the eye, that it is usually permanent, and that delayed skin necrosis can occur [1]. It notes that fillers are not approved for some body areas [1].

Forum participants acknowledge risks as well: the guide mentions vascular occlusion and instructs readers to recognise its signs [2], and a reply in a separate thread about fat-dissolving injections warns that nerve damage is a risk that can outweigh the saving [4].
No studies found. Published reviews and trials of dermal fillers concern injection by trained clinicians.

Some forum users say they spent weeks studying facial anatomy before planning self-injection [4]. Other forum users advise using a clinic, citing risks such as nerve damage [4]. The community also contains minors asking about the practice [3].

lore.intro: The practice is discussed on looksmax.org through how-to guides, shopping reports and requests for approval, sometimes with disclaimers distancing the author from encouraging it [2][4].

claims.claim: Filler can be self-administered safely if the injector studies anatomy and follows safety rules.
claims.believers: A forum guide presents rules such as slow, small deposits and knowing the signs of vascular occlusion, and a poster says he spent weeks studying facial anatomy [2][4].
claims.experts: Reference sources describe blindness and tissue necrosis as rare but serious complications of filler injection and state that US regulation requires a provider to perform injections [1]. No study of self-injection was identified.

claims.claim: Filler gives a cheap way to add jaw or chin structure that mimics surgery.
claims.believers: Posters describe using firmer and softer fillers in combination to add structure and contour, and one poster lists the products he ordered for chin work [2][4].
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes that wrinkle fillers are temporary and typically last about six months [1]. No published study assesses the results of self-injected filler.
